stories.head: Russian drone kills 14 at Dnipro station as Oleshky truce holds
stories.say: A Russian drone killed at least fourteen people at Dnipro's main railway station on Thursday, while a six-day local ceasefire around occupied Oleshky held for a third day.
stories.stand: A jet-powered drone hit a platform where two trains stood, as a local ceasefire around occupied Oleshky entered its third day.
body: A Russian drone strike on the main railway station in Dnipro, central Ukraine, killed at least 14 people on Thursday, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

He said at least 14 more were injured, six of them critically, including an 11-year-old boy. State rail company Ukrzaliznytsia said a jet-powered drone hit a platform as a train prepared to leave for Zaporizhzhia.

Separate Russian strikes killed two 15-year-old girls in Chernihiv and three people in Kremenchuk. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the Dnipro attack horrific and said sanctions on Moscow should not be eased.

Around occupied Oleshky, officials on both sides said a six-day local ceasefire that began on Tuesday was holding. It is meant to let aid reach about 2,000 people trapped in the town, and the White House said Melania Trump helped broker it.

stories.head: Italian EU force helicopter crash in Bosnia kills four
stories.say: An Italian Chinook helicopter serving with the EU's peacekeeping force crashed near Brčko in Bosnia on Thursday, killing two soldiers and two Red Cross volunteers.
stories.stand: An Italian Chinook on an EUFOR training flight came down near Brčko with 15 aboard; the cause is under investigation.
body: Four people were killed on Thursday when an Italian military helicopter serving with EUFOR, the EU's peacekeeping force, crashed near Brčko in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The CH-47 Chinook had 15 people aboard and was on what EUFOR called a routine training flight. Italy's defence ministry said the dead were two Italian soldiers and two volunteers from the Italian Red Cross's military corps.

EUFOR said the 11 injured were in a stable condition. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto offered condolences to the families. EUFOR and the Italian defence ministry are investigating, and no cause has been given.
EUFOR has been in Bosnia since 2004, overseeing the Dayton agreement that ended the 1992–1995 war.

stories.head: French prosecutors say shooting suspect targeted Muslims and Africans
stories.say: French anti-terrorism prosecutors said on Thursday that a man charged over a deadly drive-by shooting west of Paris admitted targeting people who appeared Muslim or African.
stories.stand: A 39-year-old faces terror-linked murder charges over a drive-by shooting west of Paris that killed one person and injured seven.
body: France's anti-terrorism prosecutors said on Thursday that a man accused of a drive-by shooting west of Paris admitted targeting people who appeared to be Muslim, African or North African.

The 39-year-old was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise. The shooting on 23 October, in Trappes and La Verrière, killed a 26-year-old man and injured seven people. A child was among the victims.

Prosecutor Olivier Christen said the suspect first disputed the racist nature of the attack, then changed his position on Thursday. He said the man chose the area because he saw it as a hotbed for Islamists.
Christen said a search of the man's home found brass knuckles, a bayonet and a silencer, and that he had bought parts in September to upgrade a submachine gun.

stories.head: Iran's Guards say tankers hit mines in Hormuz as Vance writes to Tehran
stories.say: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that three tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, as JD Vance reportedly wrote to Iran's security chief.
stories.stand: The IRGC blamed ships using an unauthorised route, while JD Vance reportedly wrote to Iran's security chief about possible talks.
body: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Thursday that three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. It said the ships had used an unauthorised southern route and switched off their navigation systems.
No ship names, flags or casualty figures were given. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a vessel on fire nine nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman.

US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the Wall Street Journal reported. Donald Trump said the contact was mainly about medical supplies and denied telling Vance to pursue peace talks.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran was still giving diplomacy a chance. According to the Wall Street Journal, Washington has told Gulf states to prepare for a possible new campaign after the 3 November midterms.

stories.head: Houthis say Saudi strikes kill 12 in Yemen as blasts heard in Riyadh
stories.say: Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday that Saudi strikes on homes in Taiz province killed twelve people, as at least eight explosions were heard over the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
stories.stand: The Houthis reported deaths in Taiz province and claimed six attacks on Saudi targets; the coalition says it intercepted two missiles.
body: Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday that Saudi strikes on homes in Taiz province killed 12 people and critically injured three, according to a health ministry statement carried by their Saba news agency. The coverage carried no Saudi response to the claim.

AFP reporters heard at least eight explosions in Riyadh, and authorities warned of a hostile aerial threat. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said air defences destroyed two ballistic missiles fired towards the capital.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed six attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and a military headquarters, with no independent confirmation. Saudi civil defence said shrapnel from an interception wounded one person in Riyadh.
The two sides have traded daily attacks since a truce collapsed in July. UN figures show more than 1,600 people killed in Yemen since hostilities resumed.

stories.head: North Korea fires about 10 ballistic missiles and shows off attack drones
stories.say: North Korea fired about ten ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, as Kim Jong Un watched drone and rocket tests and called for absolute superiority in drones.
stories.stand: Seoul tracked the missiles from Wonsan as Kim Jong Un watched drone and rocket tests and called for drone superiority.
body: North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area towards the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said. They flew about 250km.

State media KCNA said Kim Jong Un watched tests of suicide attack drones, cruise missiles and a 600-mm multiple rocket launcher shown in public for the first time. He called for absolute superiority in drone technology, KCNA reported.

Seoul's National Security Office called the launches a serious violation of UN Security Council resolutions. Japan's Defence Ministry said the object did not appear to land in its exclusive economic zone.

Tensions have risen since mine blasts in the Demilitarised Zone wounded three South Korean soldiers on 21 September. North Korea denies responsibility. Its previous ballistic missile launch was on 12 October.

stories.head: Erin Patterson loses appeal and is sentenced to life without parole
stories.say: Erin Patterson lost her appeal against her mushroom murder convictions in Victoria on Friday, and judges increased her sentence to life in prison without parole.
stories.stand: Victoria's Court of Appeal upheld her mushroom murder convictions and granted the prosecution's bid for a harsher sentence.
body: Erin Patterson lost her appeal against her convictions for murdering three relatives with a beef Wellington lunch laced with death cap mushrooms, Victoria's Court of Appeal ruled on Friday. She was also convicted of attempting to murder a fourth.

The court upheld the prosecution's appeal against her sentence. She had been given life with a 33-year non-parole period in September 2025. The judges removed the non-parole period, so she will not be eligible for release.

Justice Stephen McLeish said the offending was so calculated that fixing a non-parole period was inappropriate. The court rejected arguments over jurors sharing a hotel with a police witness and over mobile phone evidence.
Patterson has 28 days to decide whether to seek leave to appeal to the High Court of Australia, her last remaining route.

stories.head: Three bodies found in sunken drilling rig off Gabon, two still missing
stories.say: Search teams found three bodies on Wednesday inside the Prospector Five drilling rig that sank off Gabon, and two of the one hundred and fifteen people aboard are still missing.
stories.stand: The Prospector 5 jack-up rig sank on 24 October with 115 aboard; 110 were rescued and an investigation is under way.
body: Search teams using underwater robots found three bodies on Wednesday inside the Prospector 5, a drilling rig that sank off southern Gabon, the head of Gabon's navy said. Two people are still missing.
The jack-up rig, operated by Borr Drilling, had 115 people on board when it sank on the evening of 24 October. Officials said 110 were rescued.
Borr said the rig lost stability when one of its legs punched through the seabed during preload operations. It was preparing a drilling campaign for BW Energy in the Dussafu licence area.
Petroleum Minister Clotaire Kondja ordered a technical investigation, and a judicial inquiry has also been opened. The bodies have not yet been identified.

stories.head: US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over support for M23 rebels
stories.say: The US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry and a Rwandan savings bank on Wednesday, accusing Kigali of sending thousands of troops to back M23 rebels in eastern Congo.
stories.stand: Washington says Rwandan troops fight alongside M23 in eastern Congo despite a US-brokered peace deal; Rwanda has long denied backing the group.
body: The US Treasury imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry on Wednesday, accusing it of deploying thousands of troops in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo to support the M23 rebel group.

It also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution it says helped facilitate that support. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops.
The US sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force earlier this year. Fighting has continued despite peace accords signed in Washington by the leaders of Rwanda and Congo.
Rwanda has long denied backing M23. Congo's foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions.

stories.head: King Charles in Guyana as Caribbean calls for slavery reparations grow
stories.say: King Charles arrived in Guyana on Thursday and was greeted by President Irfaan Ali, who has said a British apology for slavery should be the next step.
stories.stand: President Irfaan Ali, who has asked for an apology for slavery, greeted the King on the second stop of a nine-day Caribbean tour.
body: King Charles arrived in Georgetown, Guyana, on Thursday and was greeted by President Irfaan Ali, on the second stop of a nine-day Caribbean tour that began in the Bahamas. It is his first visit to Guyana since 2000.
Ali has publicly asked for an apology for slavery. He told ITV News that the King had rightly recognised slavery as among the darkest days in history, and that an apology was the next step.

In Nassau on Wednesday, protesters demanded reparations. The Caribbean Reparations Commission, led by Sir Hilary Beckles, is seeking reparations from Britain, and the British government has consistently rejected calls for an apology or reparations.
The King is due in Antigua and Barbuda on Friday for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where leaders of 56 member states will gather.

stories.head: Three killed as two helicopters collide near Oregon airport
stories.say: Two helicopters collided near McMinnville airport in Oregon on Thursday, killing all three people aboard, including a student pilot from the United Kingdom.
stories.stand: A Robinson R22 and an Airbus H125 collided near McMinnville; a student pilot from the UK was among the dead, the sheriff's office said.
body: Three people were killed on Thursday afternoon when two helicopters collided in mid-air near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon, about 35 miles southwest of Portland.

The Yamhill County Sheriff's Office said a Robinson R22 carried a flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom. The pilot of an Airbus H125, a man from Newberg, Oregon, was alone on board.
The aircraft came down in a field and Highway 233 was closed. The airport manager said both helicopters were based at the airport, which stayed open.
The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation with the FAA. No cause has been given.

stories.head: US expels Cuban UN diplomat after General Assembly altercation
stories.say: The US has expelled a Cuban diplomat at the United Nations who allegedly swatted at an American official's phone during a heated General Assembly session on Tuesday.
stories.stand: Washington told Cuba's UN mission its first secretary was unwelcome after he allegedly swatted at a US official's phone during an embargo debate.
body: The US State Department has told Cuba's mission to the United Nations that its first secretary, Richard Tur de la Concepción, is no longer welcome in the country, EFE reported, citing The New York Times.
He is accused of swatting at the phone of a US official who was filming him during a General Assembly session on Tuesday. US Ambassador Mike Waltz accused him of trying to intimidate UN staff.

The session came before a vote on the US embargo on Cuba, during which Waltz accused Cuba's leaders of corruption and Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez accused him of lying. Cuba's UN ambassador filed a formal protest, saying Waltz had harassed the diplomat.
The resolution against the embargo passed with 130 votes in favour, 17 against and 25 abstentions, down from more than 160 votes in favour last year.

stories.head: Met refers itself to watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
stories.say: The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police watchdog over a 2019 letter about Thomas Markle, which it passed to the Sussexes' office without telling other agencies.
stories.stand: Scotland Yard wants a review of how it handled a 2019 letter about Thomas Markle that it passed to the Sussexes without alerting other police forces.
body: The Metropolitan Police has voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct over its handling of a letter containing allegations about Thomas Markle, the Duchess of Sussex's father.
The force said the letter reached its Protection Command in January 2019. It was addressed to the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre, and its author said it concerned the duchess's security.

The Met said the letter held no security information but did include claims about alleged offending outside the UK. It was passed to the Sussexes' office and not shared with other law enforcement agencies. Both decisions are covered by the referral.
Commander Adam Slonecki said the Met would refer the allegations to overseas agencies in the coming days. Thomas Markle denies the allegations, and police in the Philippines are investigating.

stories.head: Nuclear police rehearse armed attack on Dounreay material convoy
stories.say: Civil Nuclear Constabulary officers have rehearsed an armed attack on a lorry carrying nuclear material from Dounreay, and the nuclear regulator rated their response adequate.
stories.stand: A never-before-tested scenario saw officers foil a staged attempt to steal nuclear material, with the Office for Nuclear Regulation rating it adequate.
body: The Civil Nuclear Constabulary says its officers at Dounreay have completed their most ambitious regulatory evaluation exercise, which the Office for Nuclear Regulation rated adequate.

In the scenario, a lorry carrying a flask of nuclear material to rail transport at Georgemas Junction was stopped by a staged car crash and attacked by armed offenders. Officers also arrested a site staff member after information from an insider.
The force said officers neutralised the threat within minutes. NRS Dounreay, Highland Council and Police Scotland were among those taking part, and a recovery workshop followed the next day.
Exercise and Resilience Manager Steve Warren said the scenario had not been exercised or tested before.

stories.say: Laura Brand told her husband Russell Brand's rape trial on Thursday that he is caring and kind, but said he slept with other women when they first dated.
stories.stand: Laura Brand gave evidence for the defence at Southwark Crown Court, where her husband denies rape and sexual assault charges.
body: Laura Brand told Russell Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday that her husband was caring and kind. She said he slept with other women when they first dated in 2006 and 2007.
She said they met in August 2006, reconnected in 2015 and married in 2017, and that they have three children. Statements from two of his former girlfriends were also read to the jury.
Brand denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. He gave evidence on Wednesday, telling jurors that consent is non-negotiable.
After the prosecution objected to a question about the allegations, the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, noted she was not an expert witness. The trial resumes on Friday.

stories.head: Man admits murdering woman found drowned in Henley-on-Thames
stories.say: Nelio Gouveia, forty-two, has pleaded guilty to murdering a forty-four-year-old woman who drowned in Henley-on-Thames in March, and will be sentenced on the twentieth of November.
stories.stand: Nelio Gouveia pleaded guilty at Oxford Crown Court to the murder of a Microsoft account manager who drowned in March.
body: Nelio Gouveia, 42, of Henley-on-Thames, has pleaded guilty to murder at Oxford Crown Court, according to Oxford Daily.
The victim, a 44-year-old Microsoft account manager, died at Phyllis Court Drive in the town on 6 March. Medical evidence established that she drowned.
Gouveia was charged on 8 March and has been remanded in custody. He is due to be sentenced at the same court on 20 November.
Detective Inspector Rob Underhill of Thames Valley Police described his actions as heinous and said he was pleased Gouveia had pleaded guilty.

stories.head: Three jailed for sectarian attack on Celtic fan outside Ibrox
stories.say: Three men from Northern Ireland were jailed on Wednesday for a sectarian attack on a Celtic fan outside Ibrox, which left him with a bleed on the brain.
stories.stand: Three Northern Ireland men were jailed and given seven-year football banning orders after an assault that knocked a Celtic supporter unconscious.
body: Three men from Northern Ireland were jailed at Glasgow Sheriff Court on Wednesday for an attack on a 48-year-old Celtic supporter outside Ibrox after a Scottish Cup quarter-final on 8 March.
Scott Dragsness, 55, received 18 months. Ben Stanex, 24, and Andrew Graham, 21, each received 12 months. All three were given seven-year football banning orders.

They had pleaded guilty to assault to severe injury and danger of life. Prosecutors said the attack was a hate crime motivated by religious prejudice. The victim was knocked unconscious and suffered a bleed on the brain.
A police drone monitoring fans recorded the whole attack. Sheriff Andrew McIntyre said custody was needed to protect the public and deter others.

stories.head: Inquest finds failure to detain psychotic driver contributed to fatal crash
stories.say: A Birmingham coroner has found that failing to detain Mohammed Ali during a psychotic relapse contributed to the crash in which he killed a father the next day.
stories.stand: No police officer attended a hospital call about Mohammed Ali for eight hours the day before he drove into a parked car at about 90mph.
body: A Birmingham coroner has found that a failure to detain and assess Mohammed Ali during an acute psychotic relapse contributed to a crash that killed a 32-year-old father, ITV News reported on Wednesday.

Police were called on 17 February 2024 after Ali assaulted staff at Woodbourne Priory hospital in Edgbaston. The call was graded for a 15-minute response, but the coroner found there were insufficient resources, and no officer attended in the following eight hours.
The next evening, Ali drove his Audi at about 90mph into the back of a parked car on Soho Road, Handsworth. He was jailed for seven years in April after admitting causing death by dangerous driving.
Coroner Louise Hunt issued a Prevention of Future Deaths report. The IOPC had earlier found West Midlands Police's handling of the calls acceptable.

stories.head: Kyle Line to close for three weeks for £9m Network Rail works
stories.say: The Kyle Line between Dingwall and Kyle of Lochalsh will close from the twenty-eighth of November to the eighteenth of December for nine million pounds of work.
stories.stand: No trains will run between Dingwall and Kyle of Lochalsh from 28 November to 18 December, with buses replacing services.
body: Network Rail says the Kyle Line between Dingwall and Kyle of Lochalsh will close from 28 November to 18 December for a £9 million renewal and maintenance programme.
Buses will replace trains, and normal services are expected to resume on 19 December. Work is also planned at platforms 5 and 6 at Inverness station.

About 7km of track is to be renewed, along with drainage work on culverts and bridge repairs including the Carron Viaduct. Route director Gary Hopkirk said the line is an important connection for communities and visitors.

stories.head: Budget adds further 2-point rise to landlords' rental income tax
stories.say: Wednesday's Budget raised tax on landlords' rental income by a further two points from April 2027, to twenty-four, forty-four or forty-nine per cent, depending on tax band.
stories.stand: From April 2027 landlords will pay 24%, 44% or 49% on rental income, and property industry figures warn rents could rise.
body: Chancellor John Healey's Budget on Wednesday raised income tax on rental income by a further 2 percentage points from April 2027, on top of a rise already announced by Rachel Reeves.
Landlords will pay 24%, 44% or 49%, depending on their tax band, according to Propertymark and The Negotiator.

City AM reported that the Office for Budget Responsibility had warned the tax would push rents up nationally. Tom Bill of Knight Frank said it would put downward pressure on supply and upward pressure on rents.
Timothy Douglas of Propertymark called it a further disincentive for would-be landlords.

stories.head: £4.7bn Your First Home scheme offers buyers 2.5% deposit route
stories.say: A new four point seven billion pound scheme, Your First Home, will offer first-time buyers government equity loans on new-build homes with deposits from two point five per cent.
stories.stand: The Budget's equity loan scheme for first-time buyers takes full applications from February 2027, with first loans expected from April 2027.
body: The Budget announced Your First Home, a £4.7bn government equity loan scheme for first-time buyers, according to Propertymark and The Negotiator.
Buyers will need a deposit of at least 2.5%. Household incomes are capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in London. Price caps are £650,000 in inner London and £500,000 in outer London.

Propertymark said pre-registration opens by the end of December 2026, with full applications from February 2027 and first loans expected from April 2027. The Negotiator said the scheme is for new-build homes.
A First Time Buyer ISA launches for new savers in April 2029. Propertymark said the OBR expects only a marginal effect on housing supply.

stories.head: Mortgage approvals for house purchases fall to lowest since late 2023
stories.say: Mortgage approvals for house purchases fell again in September, to fifty-three thousand four hundred and forty-three, the lowest since December 2023, as mortgage rates kept rising.
stories.stand: Bank of England figures show 53,443 house-purchase approvals in September, a third monthly fall, while remortgaging rose.
body: Mortgage approvals for house purchases fell to 53,443 in September, the lowest monthly figure since December 2023, according to Bank of England data reported by ITV News.
City AM said it was a third consecutive monthly fall. Remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000 in August, ITV reported.
The effective interest rate on newly drawn mortgages rose to 4.63% from 4.6%. ITV said mortgage rates have kept rising, linked to the conflict in the Middle East, and markets expect a rate rise.
Katie Clinton of KPMG UK said the fall reflected ongoing strain on household finances.

stories.head: Israel's final count leaves Netanyahu bloc short as Arab parties hold balance
stories.say: Final results give Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc fifty-three of the Knesset's hundred and twenty seats, eight short of a majority, while Arab parties won a record nineteen.
stories.stand: Likud is the largest party, but neither bloc reaches 61 seats without the Arab parties, and Likud's fraud claims are disputed by election officials.
body: Final results from Israel's Central Elections Committee on Thursday gave Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, eight short of a majority. His Likud party won 27 seats, more than any other.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48 seats, 21 of them for his Yashar party. Two Arab lists won a record combined 19 seats: 11 for the Joint List and 8 for Ra'am.

Likud has accused the Arab parties of stealing the election. Committee director Dean Livne said claims of systematic violations had no basis. Committee chairman Noam Sohlberg asked Shin Bet chief David Zini to examine complaints of foreign interference, which Israeli media say include suspected Qatari funding to raise Arab turnout. Qatar denies the claims.

President Isaac Herzog must consult the parties before choosing who will try to form a government, and has urged leaders to avoid another election. The new Knesset is due to be sworn in on 10 November.

stories.head: Trump cancels Kansas and Iowa rallies and switches to tele-rallies
stories.say: Donald Trump has cancelled weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa days before Tuesday's midterms and will phone in to events across about twenty states instead.
stories.stand: Trump dropped weekend stops in Salina and Dubuque and will join tele-rallies in at least 19 states before Election Day on 3 November.
body: Donald Trump on Thursday cancelled a rally in Salina, Kansas, planned for Saturday, and another in Dubuque, Iowa, planned for Sunday.

MAGA Inc., a group aligned with Trump, said it would host tele-rallies with the president in at least 19 states, including Kansas and Iowa, before Tuesday's election. Infobae reported that the Republican National Committee presented the change as a way to extend his reach in the final days.

Trump told reporters he did not feel he had to go to Kansas, saying Senator Roger Marshall, who faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, was doing very well. Asked whether he was tired of travelling, he said he felt perfect.
Trump has held 25 rallies since 1 October. He is still expected to campaign in Florida on Friday. The midterms on 3 November will decide control of the Senate and House.

stories.head: CNN polls put Democrats ahead in Kansas, Maine, Texas and Michigan Senate races
stories.say: New CNN polls show Democratic Senate candidates ahead in Kansas, Maine, Texas and Michigan, with the Kansas and Maine leads of four points inside the margin of error.
stories.stand: Democratic challengers lead by four to seven points among likely voters days before Tuesday's midterms, though Kansas and Maine are within the margin of error.
body: Polls for CNN conducted from 20 to 27 October found Democratic Senate candidates ahead among likely voters in four states, days before Tuesday's midterm elections.

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton had 49% to 45% for Republican Senator Roger Marshall. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson had 49% to 45% for Republican Senator Susan Collins. Both leads are within the 4.5-point margin of error.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico led Republican Ken Paxton by 49% to 43%. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed led Republican Mike Rogers by 49% to 42%.
Fox News reported that at least 12.5% of Maine voters said they could still change their minds. CNN's August poll had Jackson ahead by 3 points, The Hill reported.

stories.head: Alaska governor orders inquiry into same-name Senate candidate as DOJ widens probe
stories.say: Alaska's governor has ordered state police to investigate an alleged effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the Senate ballot, as the Justice Department issues new subpoenas.
stories.stand: Mike Dunleavy asked state investigators to examine whether a Democrat-linked recruitment effort broke the law; Mary Peltola's campaign denies any involvement.
body: Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, has directed the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether an effort to recruit a candidate sharing Senator Dan Sullivan's name broke state law. He said the inquiry would decide whether criminal charges or civil action were warranted.

It follows a New York Times report on 28 October, citing emails and texts, that people associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign sought candidates who could draw votes from Sullivan. Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee deny any connection.

CBS News reported that the Justice Department has issued new subpoenas to several Democratic officials in a criminal investigation. No one has been charged. The department also amended a civil lawsuit, which seeks to block certification in some circumstances if Sullivan loses, to add a conspiracy claim. Alaska officials have asked a judge to dismiss it.

The other candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, is on the ballot with no party and says he genuinely wants to run. Donald Trump has called for him and Peltola to be removed from the ballot.

stories.head: Hegseth fires Pentagon's top military planner over alleged leaks
stories.say: Pete Hegseth has fired Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, the Joint Staff's top planner, who officials say failed three polygraph tests over alleged leaks of classified information.
stories.stand: Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, head of the Joint Staff's strategy and plans directorate, is accused of leaking classified material; the case has gone to the Justice Department.
body: Pete Hegseth, who leads the Pentagon, has removed Army Lt Gen Brett Sylvia as director of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, known as the J5. The Atlantic first reported the move.

Officials told CBS News and Fox News that Sylvia was accused of leaking classified information about the Iran war and Russia's war in Ukraine, and that he failed three polygraph tests. The case has been referred to the Justice Department. Sylvia had not responded to Fox News.

Sylvia is the second J5 head removed under Hegseth. Nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other senior leaders have been fired, pushed out or otherwise left during his tenure, most without public explanation. Hegseth has ordered a 20% cut in top officer posts by 1 January 2027.
Democratic Senator Mark Kelly accused Hegseth of purging a generation of leaders. A Joint Staff spokesperson thanked Sylvia for 32 years of service.

stories.head: China's Communist Party expels a record 33 officials at Xi's plenum
stories.say: A key Communist Party meeting in Beijing ended on Thursday with a record thirty-three senior officials expelled, sixteen of them from the military, as Xi Jinping stressed party discipline.
stories.stand: Former top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were among those expelled, and attendance fell below 300 for the first time under Xi Jinping.
body: A four-day closed meeting of China's Communist Party Central Committee ended in Beijing on Thursday with 33 senior officials expelled, a record for a single meeting, PTI reported, citing the official communique.
Sixteen of the 33 were from the military, among them former top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Former International Department head Liu Jianchao was also removed from the Central Committee.

General Zhang Shengmin, who led military anti-corruption work, was promoted to the Politburo. The party said it would keep turning the knife inwards to curb disorder, and Xi Jinping, 73, presented a draft resolution on party self-governance.
Only 279 Central Committee members and alternates attended, the first time under Xi that attendance fell below 300. The party's next congress is due in the second half of 2027.

stories.head: Albanian opposition MPs set off smoke flares in parliament
stories.say: Albanian opposition MPs set off smoke flares in parliament on Thursday and blocked the podium during a central bank vote, as protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama continue.
stories.stand: Democratic Party MPs disrupted a vote on central bank legislation amid student-led protests demanding Edi Rama's resignation; four were expelled from the chamber.
body: Opposition Democratic Party MPs set off smoke flares in Albania's parliament on Thursday and blocked the podium during a vote on central bank legislation. Governing Socialist Party MPs carried on with the vote.

Opposition members held up photographs of protesters they said had been injured by police, a claim not independently verified. Four opposition MPs were expelled from the chamber, Africanews reported. Party leader Sali Berisha's microphone was cut off during a speech attacking the government.

Student-led protests since 13 October have demanded that Prime Minister Edi Rama resign, citing alleged corruption, underfunded schools and unemployment. Rama has blamed foreign forces opposed to Albania joining the European Union.
On 22 October, opposition MPs threw objects at the Speaker, Niko Peleshi. Another demonstration is planned for Saturday.

stories.head: Healey backs away from cutting the welfare bill before the next election
stories.say: John Healey said on Thursday morning the benefits bill would come down, but by the evening said no timetable had been set, a line backed by the Treasury and Downing Street.
stories.stand: Hours after saying the benefits bill would fall, the Chancellor said no schedule had been set, and No 10 said nothing was promised for this Parliament.
body: Chancellor John Healey said on BBC Radio 4 on Thursday morning that the benefits bill would come down, though not through crude cuts.

That evening he told Channel 4 News it was wrong to say the government had set any schedule for doing so. The Treasury said he had never said welfare spending would fall in this Parliament. Downing Street said the same, and a spokesman for Prime Minister Andy Burnham said no timetable had been set.

Burnham said on a visit to Rolls-Royce in Derby that he wanted welfare spending cut as quickly as possible, but gave no timescale. The Office for Budget Responsibility expects benefits spending to rise by almost 30% to £431bn by 2032, The Telegraph reported.

stories.say: Overseas firms winning UK defence contracts worth more than fifty million pounds will have to invest back into Britain under a new policy starting in April twenty twenty-seven.
stories.stand: A new Ministry of Defence offsets policy covers contracts over £50m from April 2027, with benefits worth up to the contract's value.
body: The Ministry of Defence announced on Friday a new offsets policy requiring overseas firms that win UK defence contracts worth more than £50m to invest benefits back into Britain.

Those benefits can match the contract's value and may include jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers, technology transfer or more UK-made parts. A new Offset Authority will agree and monitor the commitments.

The policy will apply to selected procurements from April 2027. The government said more than £35.2bn had been spent on overseas defence contracts and services since 2016, 11% of the department's direct spending with industry.
The policy was announced at BAE Systems in Scotstoun, Glasgow. Poland, Norway and the Netherlands already use similar schemes.

stories.say: Christine Lagarde will leave the European Central Bank on the seventh of February, nine months early, saying she can't stay neutral, as the bank held rates on Thursday.

body: Christine Lagarde will step down as president of the European Central Bank on 7 February 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term ends in October 2027. The ECB announced the decision on Thursday.
Lagarde told reporters she did not think she could remain neutral, as central bankers are expected to be. She took office in November 2019, after leading the International Monetary Fund from 2011.

European Council President António Costa said the process to choose her successor would start on Thursday. EU leaders appoint the president by qualified majority after a recommendation from finance ministers. Euronews named Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot as frontrunners.
On the same day the ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.5%. Eurozone inflation was 3.8% in September, against a 2% target. Lagarde will chair the remaining policy meetings in December and February.

body: The Bank of Japan kept its short-term policy rate at 1.25% on Friday, at the end of a two-day meeting. The vote was 8-1, with board member Hajime Takata proposing a rise to 1.5%.

body: Utah has filed criminal charges against the prediction market Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. The complaint was filed in a Salt Lake City court on Wednesday.

The 14 counts include 12 third-degree felony counts of online gambling promotion and one second-degree felony count of pattern of unlawful activity, the Deseret News reported. The charges are allegations and have not been tested in court.

Prosecutors allege Kalshi took bets from an undercover investigator on sports events, including NFL games. Attorney General Derek Brown said gambling is illegal in Utah, whether someone places the bet, runs the game or promotes it.

A Kalshi spokesperson said it is a federally regulated exchange and no single state should have a veto over it. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to block enforcement, arguing prediction markets fall under federal jurisdiction.

stories.head: Trump declares robot and machinery imports a national security threat
stories.say: President Trump has declared imports of robots and industrial machinery a threat to national security, ordering trade talks with partners but no immediate tariffs.
stories.stand: A Section 232 proclamation orders talks with trading partners rather than immediate tariffs, with a progress report due within 180 days.
body: President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Wednesday finding that imports of robots, industrial machinery and their parts threaten US national security. It was issued under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
No tariffs were imposed for now. The Commerce Secretary and the US Trade Representative must negotiate agreements with trading partners, according to the White House.
The Herald Business reported that progress must be reported within 180 days, which DroneXL put at 26 April 2027. Tariffs or quotas could follow depending on the talks.

The White House said the US produces less robotics and industrial equipment than it uses and relies on imports for most types. The move follows earlier Section 232 actions on steel, cars, semiconductors and drones.

stories.head: MEPs tell Beijing its export model is not sustainable for Europe
stories.say: Twelve European lawmakers in China said its export model is unsustainable for Europe, with the EU's trade deficit with China at a record three hundred and sixty billion euros.
stories.stand: A 12-member European Parliament delegation pressed China to curb cheap exports, as the EU's trade deficit with China hit a record €360bn.
body: Twelve members of the European Parliament visited China from 26 to 29 October and urged Beijing to rein in cheap exports to Europe. They met Wang Wentao, China's counterpart to EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.

Pascal Canfin, the Parliament's standing rapporteur on EU-China trade, said the Chinese export model was not sustainable for the EU. Trade committee chair Bernd Lange said the EU expects more sectors to follow the approach used for hybrid cars.

Under a deal earlier in October, the EU will let in 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars a year for four years under quotas. EU leaders have asked the European Commission to consider quotas and tariffs on chemicals and industrial machinery.
The EU's trade deficit with China is a record €360 billion, Euronews reported. Talks are expected to run until at least March 2027.

stories.head: Shell and TotalEnergies double profits on refining boom
stories.say: Shell and TotalEnergies roughly doubled their third-quarter profits as refining margins soared, and Shell raised its quarterly share buyback to five billion dollars.
stories.stand: Both oil majors posted their best quarterly results since 2022 as refining margins soared amid Middle East tensions, and both expanded buybacks.
body: Shell's adjusted earnings for the third quarter were $10.81 billion, nearly double the $5.43 billion of a year earlier and above analysts' forecasts, MercoPress reported, citing Reuters.
Shell raised its quarterly share buyback from $3 billion to $5 billion. Its oil and gas production fell 17% in the first nine months of the year, mainly because of disruption in Qatar.

Both companies had their best quarter since 2022, helped by refining margins almost four times higher than a year earlier amid Middle East tensions. ExxonMobil and Chevron report on Friday.

stories.head: Spacewalkers fit the space station's seventh new solar array
stories.say: Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent seven hours and eleven minutes outside the space station on Thursday, fitting the seventh of eight new solar arrays.
stories.stand: NASA's Anil Menon and Canada's Joshua Kutryk installed and unrolled a new solar array, with one more spacewalk planned to finish the upgrade.
body: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk carried out a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station on Thursday.

They installed and unrolled the seventh of eight new roll-out solar arrays, known as iROSAs, on the P4 truss. Spaceflight Now said the eight arrays should raise station power from about 160 kW to about 215 kW.

It was Kutryk's first spacewalk, making him the fifth Canadian to walk in space, and Menon's fourth. Space.com said it was the 285th spacewalk for station assembly and maintenance, and the 100th US spacewalk from the station without a shuttle docked.
No problems were reported and the crew finished ahead of schedule. The pair are due to fit the eighth and final array on a spacewalk on 5 November.

stories.head: Sahara meteorite is one of the oldest rocks known from Mars
stories.say: A study in Science on Thursday says the Martian meteorite Teghaza zero zero one formed more than four point one billion years ago and was later altered by water on Mars.
stories.stand: A Science paper led by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory dates the Sahara-found rock to more than 4.1 billion years and links it to early Martian water.
body: A Martian meteorite found in the Sahara is one of the oldest known rocks from Mars, according to a study published in Science on Thursday.

The rock, Teghaza 001, weighs nearly 800 grams. NASA said it was found in 2022 and formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the three oldest Martian meteorites known. Researchers dated zircon crystals inside it.

The study was led by Yang Liu of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, with scientists from Caltech and the University of New Mexico among others. The team says minerals in the rock were altered by underground water, pointing to an active early water cycle.

NASA said researchers identified 13 possible places of origin in Mars's cratered southern highlands. Carl Agee of the University of New Mexico said most Martian meteorites are about 200 million years old.

stories.head: Astronomers find first double ring of debris around a dead star
stories.say: Astronomers say the white dwarf J thirteen twenty-eight is circled by two rings of planetary debris, probably shaped by two surviving bodies, one possibly as large as Pluto.
stories.stand: A Nature Astronomy study reports a double gas disc around white dwarf J1328−1450, 1,600 light-years away, likely sculpted by two planetary survivors.
body: Astronomers have found two rings of planetary debris around a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a Sun-like star, according to a study in Nature Astronomy.

The star, J1328−1450, is about 1,600 light-years from Earth. The University of Warwick said it is the first double ring of gas debris seen around a white dwarf; previously known discs were single rings.

The team proposes that two surviving bodies keep the rings apart: one about the size of an asteroid and one possibly as large as Pluto. The gas contains calcium, oxygen, magnesium and iron, suggesting rocky planets were destroyed.

The study was led by Nicola Gentile Fusillo of the University of Trieste, using the Very Large Telescope in Chile. Space.com said the system may preview the fate of planets when the Sun becomes a red giant.

stories.say: SpaceX has completed engine tests on Ship forty-two and its booster, and Elon Musk says the next Starship flight, aiming to catch both stages, is targeted for November.
stories.stand: Static fires of Ship 42 and its Super Heavy booster clear the way for Flight 15, when SpaceX plans to try catching the ship for the first time.
body: SpaceX has completed static fire tests of Ship 42, the upper stage for the next Starship test flight, Flight 15. Space.com said the ship was fired on 26 and 27 October.

SpaceX described a full-duration, six-engine firing that also ran one Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn. All 33 engines on the Super Heavy booster were fired for the full planned duration on Sunday 25 October, Tesla North reported.

Elon Musk has said Flight 15 is targeted for November and that SpaceX will try to catch both the ship and the booster with the launch tower, if regulators approve. SpaceX has caught boosters before but has never tried to catch a ship.
Musk said success is not guaranteed on these first flights. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said the company expects its FAA licence to cover catches for both stages.

stories.head: IBM links two quantum chips with 99% transfer accuracy
stories.say: IBM researchers say they moved quantum information between two chips of a hundred and twenty qubits each over eighty-centimetre cables, with about ninety-nine per cent accuracy.
stories.stand: An IBM preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, reports linking two 120-qubit processors with superconducting cables, a step towards modular quantum computers.
body: IBM researchers say they have linked two 120-qubit superconducting processors with four superconducting aluminium cables, each about 80 cm long.
Quantum states moved between the chips with an average accuracy of about 99%, and a best of 99.29%, according to a preprint posted on arXiv. The work has not yet been peer-reviewed.

The Quantum Insider said logic operations between qubits on different chips were less accurate, averaging 94.75%. The links survived three warm-up and cool-down cycles, and the team also shared entanglement across the chips.

Magnetic interference degraded the cables and needed extra shielding. The team, led by Neereja Sundaresan at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center, is pursuing modular machines; IBM aims for a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.

stories.head: Long-lost heavy neutrino could explain why matter exists, physicists say
stories.say: Two physicists propose that a heavy, long-gone neutrino tipped the early universe slightly towards matter, an idea they say future gravitational-wave observatories could test.
stories.stand: A theoretical study from Southampton and IIT Kanpur suggests a heavy sterile neutrino created the imbalance between matter and antimatter.
body: Two physicists have proposed that a heavy, now-vanished particle explains why the universe contains more matter than antimatter, in a study in Physical Review Letters reported on Tuesday.
Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton and Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur model a heavy sterile neutrino that interacted almost only through gravity.
In their model, its slow decay briefly made the early universe matter-dominated, and the decays slightly favoured matter over antimatter. The idea also links to why ordinary neutrinos are so light.

The particle has not been observed. The authors say its effects could show up in primordial gravitational waves, detectable by future observatories such as LISA, and that the model predicts a mass for the lightest neutrino.

stories.head: Primordial black holes could reveal a hidden fifth dimension, theorists say
stories.say: Theorists say black holes from the early universe would be five-dimensional if a tiny extra dimension exists, and might evaporate slowly enough to survive today.
stories.stand: A Physical Review D study links tiny primordial black holes to the 'dark dimension' idea, though neither the black holes nor the dimension has been detected.
body: Black holes formed in the early universe could carry signs of a hidden fifth dimension, according to a study in Physical Review D reported by Physics World on Thursday.
The work builds on the 'dark dimension' scenario, which proposes an extra spatial dimension curled up to about one micrometre. Primordial black holes smaller than that would be five-dimensional.

The authors, including Luis Anchordoqui of Lehman College, City University of New York, and Alek Bedroya of Princeton University, say such black holes might evaporate more slowly and survive to the present day.
Neither primordial black holes nor the extra dimension has been detected. Anchordoqui called a possible link to a high-energy neutrino seen by the KM3NeT detector very speculative.

stories.stand: The French physicist shared the 1997 Nobel with Steven Chu and William Phillips, and his ENS laboratory confirmed his death.
body: Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, the French physicist who helped develop methods to cool and trap atoms with laser light, has died aged 93. Physics World said he died in Paris on 22 October.
His death was confirmed by the Laboratoire Kastler Brossel at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris, where he worked for decades, the Boston Globe reported.

He was born on 1 April 1933 in Constantine, Algeria. He shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics with Steven Chu and William Phillips. In 1995 his team cooled helium to 180 billionths of a degree above absolute zero.
He co-wrote a widely used quantum mechanics textbook and supervised Serge Haroche, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2012.

stories.head: Seabirds get jet lag that throws their sun compass off course
stories.say: A study in Science on Thursday found Manx shearwaters flying fast east or west get jet lag, which skews their sun compass and pushes them a few kilometres off course.
stories.stand: Twenty years of GPS tracking show rapid east–west flights put Manx shearwaters' body clocks out of step with the sun, causing small navigation errors.
body: Manx shearwaters get a form of jet lag that throws them slightly off course, according to a study published in Science on Thursday.
Researchers at the University of Oxford analysed about 20 years of GPS tracking data. Science News said this covered 1,045 breeding birds and 1,837 complete homeward flights from UK colonies.
The birds are thought to steer using the sun. Rapid flights east or west change local time faster than their internal clocks adjust, so they misjudge the sun's position and veer.
The error added only a few kilometres to journeys and did not stop birds getting home. The analysis was led by behavioural ecologist Patrick Lewin.

stories.stand: The Pompeii Archaeological Park says the wardrobe's contents, including coins left behind, give a view of daily life before the eruption in AD 79.
body: Archaeologists at Pompeii have recovered the contents of a wardrobe that had stayed shut since Mount Vesuvius buried the city in AD 79, the Pompeii Archaeological Park announced.

The items include cosmetics and grooming tools, an incense burner, trade-style weights and 38 bronze coins kept in a woven container. A necklace of small charms and amulets was also found, along with skeletons of mice.
The house, on Via dell'Abbondanza, was first excavated in 1912. It has been linked to a man named Cornelius Maximus, but the inscriptions behind that name have faded.
Park director Gabriel Zuchtriegel said the identity of those who lived there cannot be reconstructed with certainty. CBS News said the coins suggest the owners had no time to retrieve valuables.

stories.stand: CSIRO surveys of Patience Seamount found a huge seasonal gathering of basketwork eels weighing more than 3,500 tonnes.
body: Up to 2.8 million basketwork eels gather around a single seamount south of Tasmania, according to a study by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO.

The eels, weighing more than 3,500 tonnes in total at the peak, collect at Patience Seamount in the Huon Marine Park, about 1,100 metres deep. The study appeared in Royal Society Open Science on 28 October.
The team, led by marine scientist Ben Scoulding, used sonar surveys and deep-towed cameras between 2023 and 2025 to count the eels and tell them apart from orange roughy, which also gather there.
The gathering peaks between March and May, which the authors link to spawning. It was first filmed in a 2007 camera survey.

stories.head: Protein analysis shows Chinese fossils were Denisovans
stories.say: A study in Nature found that twenty fossils from Xujiayao in northern China were Denisovans, giving the clearest picture yet of how the extinct human relatives looked.
stories.stand: Ancient proteins identified the Xujiayao bones and teeth as Denisovan, revealing skulls that mix Homo erectus and Neanderthal-like traits.
body: Fossils excavated at Xujiayao in northern China in the late 1970s belonged to Denisovans, according to a study in Nature reported by Live Science.

Analysis of ancient proteins in 20 bones and teeth, dated to roughly 138,000 to 199,000 years ago, confirmed all were Denisovan. They had earlier been thought to be Neanderthals or archaic Homo sapiens.
The skulls had a low, wide braincase and thick bones like Homo erectus, while the teeth were closer to those of Neanderthals and modern humans. The researchers say the traits set Denisovans apart.
Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum, who was not involved, said the sample is still small. Denisovans were first identified in 2010 from a finger bone in a Siberian cave.

stories.say: An MSF Ebola clinic in Mongbwalu, in Congo's Ituri province, has no confirmed patients for the first time since May, even as the outbreak passes ten thousand cases.
stories.stand: A clinic in Ituri marked a small milestone while the Bundibugyo outbreak, with no approved vaccine or treatment, keeps spreading in eastern Congo.
body: Staff and residents in Mongbwalu, in Ituri province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, celebrated as the last Ebola patients left a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières.
Africanews reported that it was the first time the clinic had no confirmed cases since the outbreak was declared in May. The virus is still spreading across eastern Congo.

Congo has now recorded more than 10,000 confirmed cases and almost 5,000 deaths, with a fatality rate close to 50%. Eight provinces are affected, according to Africa CDC and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Kenya has confirmed 9 cases and 2 deaths, and Nigeria 1 case.

stories.head: Lancet paper says manosphere should be treated as a public health problem
stories.say: Academics writing in The Lancet say the online manosphere harms boys, men, women and girls, and should be regulated like tobacco advertising aimed at children.
stories.stand: Authors linked to Global 50/50 compare the manosphere's business model to the tobacco and ultra-processed food industries.
body: A paper in The Lancet argues that the manosphere, a loose commercial network of online communities built around masculinity, misogyny and male victimhood, should be treated as a public health problem.

Co-authors Professor Sarah Hawkes, of the think tank Global 50/50, and Professor Kent Buse, of Monash University Malaysia, link it to violence against women and girls, mental health problems and men avoiding help.

They say outrage is profitable, and compare the industry's tactics to tobacco and ultra-processed food firms. They call for regulating platforms rather than users, stronger moderation and better support for boys in education, work and mental health care.
Jake Richards, the UK minister for men and boys, said action was needed now, RTÉ reported. A separate Lancet study by Professor Jim Catto examined how expectations of masculinity harm men's health.

stories.head: US judge blocks Medicaid 'medically frail' definition for work rules
stories.say: A federal judge in Boston has blocked a Trump administration rule narrowing who counts as too sick to meet Medicaid work requirements, after a challenge by twenty-five states and DC.
stories.stand: Judge Richard Stearns found the narrower definition unlawful but left the work requirements, due from 1 January, in place.
body: US District Judge Richard Stearns, in Boston, ruled on Thursday that a federal definition of who is "medically frail" under new Medicaid work requirements was unlawful.

The rule, issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in June, required people with qualifying conditions to also show these significantly impaired their ability to meet the work requirements. 25 states and the District of Columbia sued.

The judge said enforcing it could remove eligible, vulnerable people from Medicaid. He found states lacked time to change their systems. The ruling does not strike down the work requirements themselves.

From 1 January, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must work or volunteer 80 hours a month, or study at least half time. CMS declined to comment, KIRO 7 reported. New York Attorney General Letitia James welcomed the ruling.

stories.head: Airlines ask CDC to rethink Ebola declaration for all US-bound flyers
stories.say: Airline groups have urged the CDC to rethink a rule from November the third making every passenger flying to the US declare they have not been in Congo in the past twenty-one days.
stories.stand: The CDC order covers all international passengers and crew, including US citizens; airlines say it is too broad and too rushed.
body: From 3 November, everyone boarding an international flight to the US must state they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the previous 21 days. The CDC order covers US citizens, permanent residents and airline crew.
Airlines must collect the statements themselves, on paper or digitally, and keep them for at least 42 days. Knowingly giving false information may lead to fines or prosecution.

Airlines for America and the International Air Transport Association, which represents more than 370 airlines, wrote separately to the CDC. They asked it to reconsider, saying the rule is too broad and systems cannot be changed in time.
Airlines for America asked for exemptions for crew and military charters, Fox News reported. The CDC has not publicly responded.

stories.head: Arizona confirms first New World screwworm case, in a dog
stories.say: Arizona has confirmed its first case of the flesh-eating New World screwworm, in a dog in Cochise County near the Mexican border, making it the third US state affected.
stories.stand: Federal officials set up an infested zone and plan sterile fly releases; health officials say the risk to people is very low.
body: Arizona officials confirmed on Wednesday the state's first case of New World screwworm, in a dog in Cochise County, which borders Mexico. A vet found the dog's back wound heavily infested with maggots.
USDA laboratories in Ames, Iowa, confirmed the parasite. The USDA is setting up a 20-km infested zone with animal movement controls, more trapping and releases of sterile flies.
Arizona is the third affected state after Texas and New Mexico, where the first US case was found in June. The Hill reported 71 confirmed cases in total, 18 of them active.

The larvae feed on living tissue and affect livestock, pets and wildlife, and less commonly people. Arizona's health department said there have been no human cases in the US and the public risk is very low.

stories.head: HHS seeks new members for court-blocked US vaccine advisory panel
stories.say: The US health department has asked for nominations to its vaccine advisory committee, which has been dormant since a judge blocked Robert F Kennedy Jr's appointees in March.
stories.stand: The move could revive the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, whose advice shapes which vaccines insurers cover.
body: The US Department of Health and Human Services published a request on Thursday for nominations to the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, The Hill reported.
The panel advises the CDC, and its recommendations help decide which vaccines insurers cover. Last year Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr removed all its members and appointed critics of vaccines.
In March, Judge Brian Murphy blocked the panel's recommendations and Kennedy's appointments, ruling that he had picked unqualified people. The committee has been dormant since.
The notice asks for a balanced range of expertise, including community perspectives. Richard Hughes IV, a lawyer for the American Academy of Pediatrics, said it played down scientific expertise.

stories.head: Flu stays low in England as RSV hospital admissions rise
stories.say: UK Health Security Agency figures show flu and Covid at low levels in England, while RSV hospital admissions rose sharply, and officials say flu usually climbs in November.
stories.stand: UKHSA's weekly winter data for 19 to 25 October show RSV increasing from a low base and Covid falling.
body: Flu activity in England was stable at low levels in the week to 25 October, the UK Health Security Agency said on Thursday. Lab positivity was 6.6%, against 6.4% the week before.
Covid-19 fell slightly, with positivity at 8.3%. RSV rose from a very low base: positivity reached 1.5% and hospital admissions rose sharply, to 0.52 per 100,000.
Norovirus was within expected levels, with lab reports 39.0% below the five-season average.
Dr Alex Allen, a UKHSA epidemiologist, said flu cases usually rise in November and urged eligible people to get vaccinated.

stories.head: GP surgeries lose websites and online forms after IT supplier collapses
stories.say: GP practices in England and Wales have lost websites and online consultation forms after supplier Silicon Practice went into administration, and patients are told to phone instead.
stories.stand: NHS England says the NHS App still works and is helping affected practices find replacement providers.
body: GP practices across England and Wales have had websites, online consultation tools and forms taken offline after Silicon Practice, a Leicestershire firm, entered administration, IBTimes UK reported.
The company, which traded through Schappit Ltd, said it hosted around 1,000 practice websites. Practices in London, Gloucestershire, Norfolk, Derby and Swansea Bay reported problems.
Some practices warned that forms sent shortly before the outage may not have reached clinicians. NHS England and local health boards told patients to contact practices by phone or in person.
Practices said the NHS App and SystmOnline were not affected. Patients needing urgent help are directed to NHS 111, or 999 in an emergency.

stories.head: Government backs five-day breast radiotherapy trial and names cancer adviser
stories.say: The government is highlighting a trial cutting breast cancer radiotherapy from three weeks to five days, and has made Ashley Dalton MP an adviser on the National Cancer Plan.
stories.stand: The NIHR-funded FAST-Forward Boost trial has passed 1,000 patients and aims to recruit 4,830 by 2028.
body: The Department of Health and Social Care said on Friday that more than 1,000 people have joined FAST-Forward Boost, a trial testing whether breast cancer radiotherapy, including an extra boost dose, can be given in five days rather than three weeks.
The trial, led by The Institute of Cancer Research and funded by the NIHR, aims to recruit 4,830 patients by 2028. Results are expected in 2033. Patients could be spared 10 hospital visits.
Ashley Dalton MP, who lives with incurable secondary breast cancer, has been appointed adviser on delivering the National Cancer Plan. She will work with minister James Frith.
The department said 63.6% of women took up their first screening invitation, the highest in a decade, but about four in 10 do not attend.

stories.head: Argentina's Senate approves overhaul of 2010 mental health law
stories.say: Argentina's Senate has voted forty-two to twenty-one to replace the country's 2010 mental health law, changing the rules on involuntary admissions; the bill now goes to the lower house.
stories.stand: The government-backed bill gives psychiatrists priority in care teams and adds gambling to the definition of addiction.
body: Argentina's Senate approved a bill early on Friday to replace the 2010 mental health law, by 42 votes to 21, Infobae reported. It now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

The bill changes who can sign off involuntary admissions, requiring a doctor, preferably a psychiatrist, or someone with mental health training. Psychiatrists get priority in care teams, but psychologists remain in them.
It separates adult and child care, broadens addiction to include gambling, bans asylum-style practices and allows advance treatment decisions. Telehealth is permitted where specialists are scarce.
The ruling party La Libertad Avanza backed the bill. Some provincial senators criticised the lack of a debate on funding.

stories.head: Wildfire smoke in pregnancy linked to higher autism risk, US study finds
stories.say: A Rutgers study of nearly nine hundred thousand US mothers and children links wildfire smoke during pregnancy to a higher risk of an autism diagnosis, though it cannot show cause.
stories.stand: The JAMA Pediatrics study found the strongest link for exposure in the second and third trimesters.
body: Researchers at the Rutgers School of Public Health studied 893,212 mother and child pairs enrolled in Medicaid across the contiguous United States, with children born from 2007 to 2014.

Each rise of 0.75 micrograms per cubic metre in average wildfire fine particles during pregnancy was linked to a 30% higher risk of a later autism diagnosis. The strongest links were after the 15th week.
The study, published in JAMA Pediatrics and led by epidemiologist Stefania Papatheodorou, is observational and cannot prove that smoke causes autism. It covers only Medicaid enrollees.
The authors suggest better air-quality forecasting and limiting smoke indoors to protect pregnant women.

stories.head: Tumour atlas aims to explain why bowel cancer is deadlier in young people
stories.say: Dana-Farber researchers have built a single-cell atlas of one hundred and eighty-nine bowel tumours from patients in their twenties to nineties, to study why young people fare worse.
stories.stand: The Nature Medicine study is described as the largest biological database of its kind for colorectal tumours.
body: Researchers led by Kimmie Ng, director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute's Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, published a single-cell atlas of colorectal tumours in Nature Medicine on Thursday, STAT reported.
The atlas covers 189 tumours from patients aged from their 20s to their 90s. STAT described it as the largest biological database of its kind.
Early-onset colorectal cancer, usually defined as under 50, is often diagnosed later and is harder to treat. Ng said survival may be worse for patients under 35.
The researchers say the atlas should help separate factors that confused earlier studies and point to future treatment targets.

stories.head: Weaker brain rhythm linked to timing and speech problems in schizophrenia
stories.say: McGill researchers found people with schizophrenia had weaker, slower beta-band brain activity, tied to trouble judging timing and to disorganised speech, in a small first study.
stories.stand: The Science Advances study of 50 people suggests one signal may underlie several symptoms; the authors call it preliminary.
body: Researchers at McGill University used brain scanning to compare 25 people with schizophrenia and 25 healthy volunteers, in a study published in Science Advances.

People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band brain activity. Those with the biggest changes had more trouble judging the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganised speech and more severe symptoms.
The same weak signal appeared when processing sounds, sights and movement, suggesting a shared mechanism, according to the team led by Dr Lena Palaniyappan.
The authors describe the results as preliminary and say larger studies are needed. If confirmed, the signal could help identify young people at risk of psychosis.

stories.head: Glacial lake bursts in Bhutan, forcing evacuations downstream in India
stories.say: A glacial lake in Bhutan's Gasa district burst on Thursday evening, washing away a hot spring site and sending more than six thousand people in West Bengal to safer ground.
stories.stand: Shintaphu Lake in Bhutan's Gasa district burst on Thursday, prompting flood alerts and evacuations along the Sankosh river in north-east India.
body: A glacial lake outburst flood began at Shintaphu Lake, in Bhutan's Gasa district, on the evening of Thursday 29 October. The lake sits at the source of the Mo Chhu river.

The Week reported that about 7.4 million cubic metres of water were released. The flood destroyed facilities at Gasa Tshachu, a hot spring beside the river. Bhutan said there had been no injuries or loss of life so far.

India issued flood alerts for Alipurduar in West Bengal and Dhubri in Assam, along the Sankosh river. Alipurduar police chief Amit Kumar Shaw said 4,000 to 5,000 people were in relief shelters and more than 6,000 had been moved to safer areas.
A red alert remained on the Sankosh river system. The Punatsangchhu II hydropower plant in Bhutan halted generation and opened its spillway gates, The Week reported.

stories.stand: Oil from a tanker struck near the Strait of Hormuz has shut beaches across the northern UAE and is now close to a seawater intake.
body: Oil leaking from a damaged tanker has reached the coast of the northern United Arab Emirates, closing beaches in several emirates. The environment ministry confirmed the spill on 23 October.

Reuters reported on Thursday that footage it verified showed the slick about 2 km from the Naqa'a desalination plant, on the border of Umm Al Quwain and Ras Al Khaimah. The UAE had not announced any plant shutdowns.

stories.head: Flash floods in northern and eastern Syria kill at least five
stories.say: Heavy rain across northern and eastern Syria has killed at least five people, four of them children, and five more are missing, the emergency ministry said on Thursday.
stories.stand: Floods in Raqqa and Deir Az Zor killed at least five people, cut a key road and forced families out of displacement camps.
body: At least five people have died in flash floods after heavy rain in northern and eastern Syria, the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said on Thursday.

Four children drowned in Raqqa and Deir Az Zor governorates. A man died when his car was caught by floodwater near the al-Salmani Bridge in western Raqqa. Five others, including two children, are missing.
Emergency teams rescued 15 people from trapped vehicles. The ministry evacuated about 375 families from three camps on the outskirts of Raqqa.
State news agency SANA said the al-Salmani Bridge, west of Tabqa, collapsed and closed the road linking Raqqa and Aleppo. The ministry also reported damage in Aleppo, Hasakah and Homs.

stories.say: Record sea temperatures are bringing invasive toadfish to Greek waters and a record bloom of octopus to the English Channel, upending what fishers catch.
stories.stand: Europe's seas were more than 2°C above average this summer, and fishers are reporting new arrivals that damage nets or replace familiar catches.
body: European sea surface temperatures this summer were more than 2°C above the average of the last three decades, Inside Climate News reported. The Mercator Ocean bulletin says June to August 2026 had the highest mean global sea temperature on record.
In Greece, the invasive silver-cheeked toadfish is damaging nets and eating catch in the Aegean. The agriculture ministry has offered a bounty of about €5.33 per kilo.

Common octopus arrived in the English Channel in record numbers, which the Marine Biological Association links to warmer water. It is described as the largest bloom in 75 years, and Defra held its first octopus conference in October.
A study led by Timothy Ravasi of the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology found more than 125 fish species in Japanese waters have moved north.

stories.head: Arsenic readings near Grand Canyon cluster at uranium mine, analysis says
stories.say: An analysis by the Grand Canyon Trust says three of the four wells in the region with arsenic above the federal limit are at the Pinyon Plain uranium mine.
stories.stand: A conservation group's review of 32 years of groundwater data points to the Pinyon Plain mine, which regulators and the operator say is drawing in natural arsenic.
body: The Grand Canyon Trust published an analysis on 28 October of 32 years of groundwater samples from 40 sites, using federal and Arizona data.

It found three of the four wells in the region with average arsenic above the federal drinking water standard are at the Pinyon Plain uranium mine, run by Energy Fuels. The mine is about nine miles from the South Rim.
Inside Climate News reported that water in the mine's sump is over 3,000 times the drinking water limit. Arizona regulators let the company raise the arsenic alert level at one monitoring well.

The regulator and Energy Fuels say pumping draws in naturally arsenic-rich water. The Havasupai Tribe's appeal against the limit was dismissed for lack of standing, and Chairwoman Melinda Yaiva says it is weighing other options.

stories.head: Finnish police open criminal probe into forest clearing for Google data centre
stories.say: Finnish police have opened a criminal investigation into a Google subsidiary over land clearing and drainage at a planned data centre site near Muhos.
stories.stand: Police are examining whether Tuike Finland broke the water act and caused environmental damage before required impact assessments were done.
body: Finnish police announced on Thursday a criminal investigation into Tuike Finland, a subsidiary of Alphabet's Google, over suspected breaches of environmental law.

The case concerns a planned data centre site near the town of Muhos, in northern Finland. Authorities say the company cleared forest and drained land before completing the required environmental impact assessments.
Police are examining whether the company broke the water act and caused environmental damage. A guilty finding could bring a corporate fine. Police expect to give an update in December.
Finland's supervisory agency ordered Google on 6 October to halt preparatory work at Muhos and another site. Google has said it began the works based on its understanding of the approvals required.

stories.head: African negotiators seek adaptation finance item on COP31 agenda
stories.say: The African Group of Negotiators has asked the UN climate chief to add adaptation finance, trade and Green Climate Fund financing to the agenda at COP31 in Antalya.
stories.stand: The bloc wants formal talks on tripling adaptation finance at the summit opening on 9 November, a move developed countries have resisted.
body: The African Group of Negotiators has written to UN climate chief Simon Stiell asking for three new items on the COP31 agenda, Climate Home News reported. The talks open in Antalya, Turkey, on 9 November.
The items are tripling adaptation finance, trade and climate change, and the financing arrangements of the Green Climate Fund. The group is chaired this year by Ghana.

At COP30 in Belém, governments agreed to at least triple adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, without setting a baseline or an amount. The least developed countries want a goal of $120 billion a year by 2030.
At the June talks in Bonn, the EU, UK and Japan opposed placing the tripling target in adaptation negotiations. Any government can object to an agenda item when the summit opens.

stories.head: China puts green trade at the top of its COP31 demands
stories.say: China says the COP31 climate talks in Antalya should discuss the free flow of green technology and what it calls trade protectionism, setting up a clash with the EU.
stories.stand: Beijing wants trade on the table at COP31, while the EU says the UN climate talks should not become a venue for trade disputes.
body: China's vice-minister of ecology and environment, Li Gao, has said COP31 should discuss the free flow of green technology and trade unilateralism and protectionism, Climate Home News reported.

At COP30, China, India and South Africa pushed to put unilateral trade measures on the agenda, mainly aimed at the EU's carbon border levy. China dominates global clean-tech manufacturing and opposes US and EU tariffs on its products.
The EU says the UN trade dialogue should not become a venue for trade disputes. The UK plans its own carbon border mechanism from January.
Experts polled by Carbon Brief said upholding multilateralism is likely to be Beijing's top priority. One expected China to resist linking electrification targets to fossil fuel phase-out pledges.
