stories.head: Budget forecasts assume new North Sea fields including Rosebank go ahead
stories.say: Forecasts published with Wednesday's Budget assume ministers approve new North Sea fields, including the Rosebank oilfield, which is still awaiting a decision.
stories.stand: The OBR's tax forecasts count on new North Sea fields being developed, though the Energy Secretary has not yet ruled on Rosebank.
body: Forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility, published with Chancellor John Healey's Budget, assume the Rosebank oilfield will be approved, Carbon Brief and City AM reported.

City AM said the OBR used regulator estimates assuming approval of about 1.2 billion barrels of oil and gas in untapped reserves. It expects production to fall by about 10% a year from 2027 to 2031, or by 14% without new fields.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved the Jackdaw gas field in the week before the Budget. The decision on Rosebank is still pending. A Treasury spokesperson said it would follow a separate quasi-judicial process.
The Budget also confirms an oil and gas revenue levy to replace the energy profits levy, which ends by April 2030 at the latest.

stories.head: MPs say Sizewell C funding leaves taxpayers and bill payers with the risk
stories.say: The Public Accounts Committee says bill payers could pay nine point eight billion pounds more during Sizewell C's construction if costs reach the top of their range.
stories.stand: The Commons spending watchdog says the nuclear plant's financing puts extraordinary risk on the public and wants six-monthly cost reports.
body: The Commons Public Accounts Committee published a report on Sizewell C on 28 October. It said the nuclear plant's funding model exposes taxpayers and consumers to unusually large risks.

Construction is estimated to cost £40.5bn to £47.7bn, with completion between 2039 and 2043. If costs reach the top of that range, consumers could pay £9.8bn more during construction, while private investors would add only about £30m.
Committee chair Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown called the level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers extraordinary. The government holds 44.9% of the project company.
The MPs want costs and consumer impacts reported every six months. A government response is due by 28 December. The government says the model lowers financing costs.

stories.head: Tokayev calls for faster work on Kazakhstan's nuclear power plants
stories.say: President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said building Kazakhstan's Balkhash nuclear plant could start as early as next year, and called for a long-term national uranium reserve.
stories.stand: In his state-of-the-nation address, Kazakhstan's president urged quicker progress on two planned nuclear plants to create an electricity surplus.
body: Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called on Wednesday for faster progress on two planned nuclear power plants, in his annual state-of-the-nation address to parliament.
He said construction of the Balkhash plant could begin as early as next year. He wants a cooperation agreement for the Moyynkum plant signed so building can start as soon as possible.
Tokayev also called for a long-term national uranium reserve. He said nuclear power would give the country an electricity surplus, which he called essential for digitalising the economy and using AI.
He criticised the current system, in which Kazakhstan buys electricity from neighbours at high prices in winter and sells it back cheaply in summer, Euronews reported.

stories.head: China's clean-tech exports to avoid as much CO2 as Brazil emits, analysis says
stories.say: An analysis for Carbon Brief estimates China's clean-tech exports this year will avoid about four hundred and fifty million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, roughly Brazil's emissions.
stories.stand: Exports of Chinese solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric vehicles grew sharply in 2026, with most of the climate benefit in the global south.
body: China's exports of clean technology in 2026 will avoid around 450 million tonnes of CO2 a year, according to an analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta of the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, published by Carbon Brief.

That is roughly Brazil's annual fossil CO2 emissions, and nearly 2% of global emissions outside China. Over their lifetimes, this year's exports would avoid about 8,400 million tonnes, up from 6,800 million for 2025's exports.
In the first three quarters of 2026, exports of electric cars and heavy vehicles grew 61% by this measure, wind turbines 45%, batteries 39% and solar 22%.
The analysis puts 76% of the avoided emissions in the global south, with India first and the US second.

stories.head: Binance freezes assets after suspected $6.3bn hack
stories.say: Binance says a suspected breach has affected six point three billion dollars in crypto, about three billion of it frozen, and has paused deposits and withdrawals.
stories.stand: The world's largest crypto exchange says users' funds are safe and it will cover all losses while it traces the stolen assets.
body: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, estimated the impact of a suspected security breach at $6.3bn. About $3bn of the affected assets had been located and frozen, it said.

The exchange said hackers may have got in through a staff member's laptop. It said it had found no evidence of a wallet private key leak, and suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks ran.

Co-founder Yi He said Binance would cover all hacking losses. Tether froze nearly $1.57bn of linked assets and Circle more than $800m. Arkham chief executive Miguel Morel said the incident began around 4:30pm EDT on Thursday.
If confirmed, it would far exceed the previous record: the theft of about $1.5bn from the exchange Bybit in February 2025, blamed on the North Korea-linked Lazarus Group.

stories.head: Nvidia rejects report that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese asset
stories.say: The New York Times reports that a Megaspeed executive US officials see as a Chinese asset grew close to Jensen Huang; Nvidia says his contacts with her were not unusual.
stories.stand: US officials reportedly believe a Megaspeed executive passed information to Beijing; Nvidia says chip diversion claims were investigated and debunked last year.
body: The New York Times reported on Thursday, citing anonymous sources, that US authorities believe Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore data centre company Megaspeed, is a Chinese asset. She is not related to Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang.

According to the report, she developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, and US spy agencies found last year that she was passing information to Beijing. The Times also reported that she arranged for Megaspeed to buy about $2bn of Nvidia chips.
President Donald Trump was reportedly briefed about a year ago and took no action. The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill.

An Nvidia spokesperson said Jensen Huang's interactions with her were not unusual or unexpected, and that customers receive only ordinary business information. The company said chip diversion claims were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.

stories.say: Polymarket briefly halted trading on its international platform on Thursday after unauthorised withdrawals, blaming a hacked outside provider, and says users will be repaid.
stories.stand: The prediction market says one external provider was compromised; reports link the breach to UK-based monitoring service DebugBear.
body: Prediction market Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday, after users reported unauthorised withdrawals and positions closed without their permission.

Polymarket said one external provider had been compromised, and that it had referred the matter to law enforcement. Reports link the breach to DebugBear, a UK-based website performance monitoring service. The company's statement did not name the vendor.

Researchers at Hudson Rock said malicious code served through the vendor's script hijacked active trading sessions. Polymarket said its core smart contracts and its separate US platform were not affected.
Trading resumed after Polymarket said the issue was fixed. The company said affected users would be fully reimbursed.

stories.head: Pentagon treats military base freezer failures as a suspected hack
stories.say: US investigators are treating freezer failures at military base food shops as a suspected cyberattack, Reuters reported on Thursday, and have spoken to French police.
stories.stand: Fridges and freezers at at least six US base commissaries went into defrost mode in August; the cause has not been confirmed.
body: Investigators are treating freezer failures at US military base commissaries as a suspected cyberattack, four officials told Reuters on Thursday. A unit of US Cyber Command is involved.

In late August, refrigerators and freezers at at least six commissaries, the on-base food shops, switched to defrost mode and warmed, spoiling food. Affected bases included Fort Huachuca in Arizona and Fort Irwin in California.

Investigators have spoken with French police, who are looking at attacks that altered cooling settings at supermarkets in France in mid-October. Danfoss, whose controllers were used in many affected French stores, said many units were old or running outdated software.
The Pentagon has not confirmed that anyone accessed commissary systems, or explained the cause.

stories.head: Icelandic host refuses DHS request to remove leaked staff data
stories.say: Homeland Security asked an Icelandic web host on Thursday to take down leaked data on its staff; FlokiNET refused, and the site moved to a new domain after a suspension.
stories.stand: DHS says the leaked database puts more than 40,000 identifiable people at risk of harassment, stalking and physical harm.
body: The US Department of Homeland Security asked Icelandic hosting company FlokiNET on Thursday to remove a leaked database of its staff, which includes ICE and CBP personnel. The request was sent through contractor ZeroFox.

The DHS letter said the data put more than 40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking and physical harm. FlokiNET refused, saying the records show work details rather than private ones.

The icepi.cx domain was suspended on Thursday, but the database soon reappeared at another address. The data was first published on Wednesday by Distributed Denial of Secrets. A group calling itself the Department of Peace claimed it obtained it.
A DHS spokesperson said the agency was aware of a potential breach and working to address it.

stories.head: GM to pay $220m over claims it sold drivers' data
stories.say: General Motors will pay two hundred and twenty million dollars to settle claims by thirty-five states and Washington DC that it sold drivers' data to brokers without permission.
stories.stand: States said driving and location data from GM's Smart Driver programme ended up with insurers, who used it to set rates.
body: General Motors agreed on Thursday to pay $220m to settle claims by the attorneys general of 35 US states and the District of Columbia over the sale of drivers' data.

The states said GM sold driving behaviour and location data to brokers, who sold it on to insurers that used it to set and sometimes raise premiums. The data came from GM's Smart Driver programme, which ran from 2016 until it ended in 2024.
Under the settlement, GM must limit the driving data it collects and get drivers' express consent before collecting or sharing it. Oregon's Dan Rayfield and Washington's Nick Brown led the coalition.
A GM spokesperson said the company was committed to being clear about what information it uses.

stories.say: South Korea's education ministry says students caught using AI glasses in the college entrance exam could face prosecution and a ban of up to three years.
stories.stand: Ahead of the 19 November exam, every test site will have an inspector checking for AI glasses.
body: South Korea's education ministry said on Thursday that students who cheat using AI glasses would face prosecution for obstructing official duties by fraudulent means.
The ministry also wants to extend the ban on retaking the national college entrance exam, the CSAT, from one year to up to three years.
For this year's exam on 19 November, one device inspector will be stationed at each test site. The ministry is also assessing radio wave detectors that could be used from next year.
AI glasses were added to the exam's list of banned items in July. The ministry will urge universities to apply tougher rules to their own entrance exams.

stories.stand: More than half of respondents said generative AI cut their working hours by at least one hour a week.
body: Staff at Japan's government ministries and agencies saved an average of 110 minutes a week using the Gennai generative AI platform, according to a Digital Agency survey released on Friday.
The survey, carried out in August and September, drew 6,439 valid responses. More than half said they had cut at least one hour a week, and 3.2% said they saved 10 hours or more.
About 34.6% said their working hours were largely unchanged. Respondents said the tool helped them draft documents quickly and find information in large volumes of text.

stories.head: Intel's budget laptop chip sells out as memory shortage hits PCs
stories.say: Intel says its Wildcat Lake chip for cheaper laptops is sold out, but warns rising memory costs are pushing up PC prices and memory supply will not improve in 2027.
stories.stand: Intel expects PC sales to keep falling, with its finance chief forecasting a weaker 2027 for laptops and desktops.
body: Intel said on its earnings call on Thursday that Wildcat Lake, its chip for entry-level laptops, is sold out. It is used in low-priced Windows 11 machines such as Dell's XPS 13 and HP's Omnibook 5 14.

Chief executive Lip-Bu Tan said PC makers had signalled a slowdown, as rising memory costs and shortages push system prices higher. He called the memory crunch, driven by AI demand, one of the most severe in the industry's history.
Finance chief David Zinsner said he did not expect memory supply to improve in 2027. He forecast PC unit sales falling about 12% in 2026.
Revenue in Intel's PC chip division fell 9% from the previous quarter, to $8.1bn.

stories.say: Sir Patrick Stewart, Captain Picard in Star Trek and Professor Xavier in X-Men, has died at his Los Angeles home aged eighty-six, after Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.
stories.stand: The Yorkshire-born Shakespearean actor became a global star as Jean-Luc Picard and later as Charles Xavier in the X-Men films.
body: Sir Patrick Stewart has died at his home in Los Angeles aged 86. A statement posted on his social media accounts said he died on Wednesday with his wife, Sunny, beside him.
The statement said his final period was a brief journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. His longtime spokesperson confirmed the death.

Born in Mirfield, Yorkshire, in 1940, he made his name on stage with the Royal Shakespeare Company. He played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994, and returned in Star Trek: Picard from 2020.

He played Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films from 2000 and was knighted in 2010. He had filmed Avengers: Doomsday, due in cinemas in December. Marvel Studios and Hugh Jackman were among those paying tribute.

stories.say: Brazil's sports court has banned Santos captain Neymar for two matches for covering his mouth while arguing with a Bahia player, a breach of the so-called Vinicius Junior rule.
stories.stand: Brazil's sports court banned the Santos captain for covering his mouth during an argument with a Bahia player, Al Jazeera reports.
body: Brazil's Superior Court of Sports Justice has banned Santos captain Neymar for two matches, Al Jazeera reported on Thursday.
The court found he broke the so-called Vinicius Junior rule, which bars players from covering their mouths during on-field confrontations.

It happened in an argument with Bahia's Rodrigo Nestor during Saturday's 1-1 Serie A draw. Neymar was sent off, and the referee's report said he then ran towards the visitors' bench and had to be restrained.
He was already suspended for a league game against Palmeiras after three yellow cards, so he will miss three matches in all. Neymar and Santos can appeal.

body: Celtic and Rangers must play their next home Scottish Cup matches behind closed doors, after a tribunal upheld the Scottish Football Association's sanctions.
The punishment followed disorder after Celtic beat Rangers on penalties in a Scottish Cup quarter-final at Ibrox. STV said fans clashed on the pitch and police made 37 arrests.
Celtic said its appeal was partially upheld. Brit Brief reported that a threat of a further closed-door game had been dropped.
Celtic called the punishment excessive and disproportionate. It said the SFA had drawn a false equivalence between the two sets of fans. Rangers had not commented, STV said.

stories.say: Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cleared of foul play by a disciplinary panel, after Munster's Gavin Coombes said he was grabbed in the groin during Saturday's match.
stories.stand: An independent disciplinary committee unanimously dismissed the citing against the Leinster and Ireland prop after Saturday's game against Munster.
body: Leinster and Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cleared of foul play. An independent disciplinary committee unanimously dismissed a citing complaint on Thursday.
Munster's Gavin Coombes told referee Andrew Brace during Saturday's United Rugby Championship match that he had been grabbed in the groin area. A TMO review found no evidence at the time.
Citing commissioner Peter Ferguson later cited Furlong under Law 9.27. The committee found no foul play, and said Coombes had given an honest account of what he remembered.
Furlong is free to play for Ireland in the Nations Championship next month, when they face sides including Argentina, Fiji and South Africa.
